extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and skeptics interested in natural theology/apologetics (18th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A natural-theology/apologetic argument that the circulation of waters, distribution of mountains, seas, rivers, salts, and related phenomena provide evidence of a wise Creator. The page assembles observational, geographical and hydrostatic points as evidentiary criteria supporting design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of vapours / evaporation rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The text treats the rate of exhalation (evaporation) from water as a measurable quantity — e.g. taking one inch a day (or half an inch) as a medium — and uses empirical observations (Dr. Halley, Miller at Purmer-meer) to estimate total vapours above the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes numerical calculations: one inch/day over whole surface, or half-inch/day leading to 90 inches/year if all exhalations fell as rain; empirical notes (Halley: surface fell 1/12 inch in 2 hours; Miller: Purmer-meer lost 15 timber-inches over given days = ~1/2 inch/day). Concludes there must be many times more vapour exhaled than descends as rain (e.g., 'there must be 43 times as much Water exhaled as descends in Rain', leaving large surplus vapours to service plants and mountains). Use of these measured/estimated figures functions as evidentiary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation of the waters (evaporation → clouds → precipitation) as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuous cycle whereby waters ascend as vapours, are preserved in clouds, and descend again in forms (mist, hail, snow, rain) is presented as a striking, purposeful circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument frames this circulation as a marvel: 'a great quantity of Vapours ascends from Water... are there preserv'd in Clouds; and passing a second time thro' the said Air, are made to descend again... and compose those great Rivers' — used as a cumulative sign of design rather than chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountains distributed and placed for producing rivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mountains are asserted to be 'distributed throughout the whole Earth' and 'mostly in the highest countries, in order to transmit these Rivers' long distances, making them apt sources for rivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated observations (I–VI) describe fitness: mountains occur in highlands to send rivers far; they are distributed to yield many rivers; the Earth's surface slopes toward seas; mountains in promontories/islands collect vapours; references to Varenius and Burnet for geographic confirmation. Treated as evidence of wise design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earth's surface adapted (gradually lower toward seas) to facilitate river flow
rubrics_metrics.description: The global surface is adapted to transmit rivers, 'which grows gradually lower on all sides where it is washed by the Sea', so water 'always runs to the lowest Places'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used with the mountains' placement to argue purposeful topography: the gradual lowering and courses of rivers (Rhine, Danube, Rhone, Borysthenes) indicate design in the Earth's shape and drainage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountains in promontories and islands positioned to capture vapours
rubrics_metrics.description: Promontories and islands often have mountains centrally placed or running through them to collect and condense vapours that would otherwise be scattered by winds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: islands such as St. Helena and St. Thomas are mentioned as being too hot to get rain without mountains; citations to Varenius and Burnet on island mountain placement. The placement is read as too useful to be accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea-salt preserves the ocean from corruption and aids terrestrial life
rubrics_metrics.description: The salt in the sea prevents putrefaction and freezing and, during evaporation, salts are left behind so precipitated water becomes useful for animals and plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that if the ocean were fresh it would stagnate and corrupt; yet vapour ascent leaves salts behind ('leave all their Salts behind them') so rain is fresh. Mentions global salt mines and salt mountains as evidence that salt is part of Earth's mineral provision — rhetorical evidence for providence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bays and gulfs formed to receive river discharge and prevent inland flooding
rubrics_metrics.description: Sea arms, bays and gulfs (e.g., Mediterranean, East-Sea, West limbs) are described as formed to receive rivers, preventing inland countries from being inundated by river discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that seas 'transmit great Branches or Arms... into the Land, in order ... to receive likewise the Tests of the Rivers Bosom'; uses geographic examples and Varenius to support the idea these features are purposive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfathomable ocean basins prepared to contain rivers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Earth contains very large and deep receptacles (the oceans) suitable to receive and hold the discharge of innumerable rivers so the land is not inundated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical point: 'Is it then by Chance, that there are prepared in the Earth such unfathomable Depths, as may contain the whole Ocean, and into which all the Rivers may discharge their Waters?' Used as a design criterion: presence of deep basins is evidence of providential arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea as facilitator of commerce and transport
rubrics_metrics.description: The seas are presented as the only practical means for carrying great burdens and enabling commerce across distant lands with little force, a benefit pointing to design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: East-India ships, Dutch commerce; rhetorical question about the alternative terrestrial machines and armies required without seas. Used to argue moral obligation/ gratitude toward Creator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic effects and ships' buoyancy as evidence of contrivance
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of a small quantity of water to raise and move enormous ships (hydrostatic laws) is adduced as a demonstration of design requiring knowledge and contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a dock thought-experiment: filling a narrow space with sea-water will raise a large ship; promises fuller treatment in laws of hydrostatics. Used to illustrate purposeful physical laws that serve mankind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-salts / saltpetre enriching water and soil
rubrics_metrics.description: Nitrous salts ('Salt-petre') produced by the air are said to make water more fructifying and to contribute to fertility; the Nile carries saltpetre that fertilizes otherwise barren lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites French Academy experiments and references (1699, 1703) showing gardeners and naturalists recognizing the fertilizing role. Presented as a designed provision for fertility and human benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific necessary conditions of the Nile's inundation (seven-point list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nile's fertility without rain depends on a specific conjunction of conditions: (1) water brought from other parts; (2) the country being lower than Nile's sources; (3) higher regions elsewhere to allow habitation; (4) sufficient volume to overflow banks; (5) water must linger to deposit slime/mud; (6) water impregnated with enough saltpetre but not too much; (7) water must run off again leaving lands dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerated list of required features is used to argue the unlikelihood of accident: 'Can any Body satisfy themselves in affirming, that this was done without Design?' Used as an inferential rubric: complexity and specificity of conditions point to purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerous fountains/springs and arrangement of brooks into rivers
rubrics_metrics.description: The widespread presence of fountains and little rills joining into great rivers, producing running and living waters that resist corruption, is read as evidence that mountains exist to supply such fresh flowing water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that if there were only large stagnant collections they would decay; the distribution of many springs and streams is functionally beneficial and thus indicative of design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vapours leave salts behind enabling fresh precipitation
rubrics_metrics.description: During ascent into air, ocean water 'leave[s] all their Salts behind them', so the resulting precipitation is fresh and suitable for drinking and agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to rebut the idea that the ocean's salinity would make rain useless: the physical process of evaporation/desalination is presented as a beneficial mechanism in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea currents and straits (Gibraltar, Dardanelles) evidence purposeful arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed currents through narrow straits and the differing ease of passage into/out of seas (e.g., Mediterranean vs. Atlantic) are noted as purposeful hydraulic arrangements allowing both reception and discharge of waters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes sailors' experience (tacking into the Mediterranean easier than leaving), local theories (sun heat, subterranean cavities), and treats the entire phenomenon as an ocular demonstration of divine direction 'after a wonderful manner.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation prevents seas from overflowing the land
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance created by evaporation and precipitation (the circulation) explains why the sea does not continually overflow the continents despite constant river discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an explanatory criterion: because river input is returned by evaporation and rainfall, the system preserves stable sea boundaries; this balance is taken as evidence of providential regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marine life adapted to sea depths and salinity as designed provision
rubrics_metrics.description: The innumerable kinds of fishes and marine creatures, their adaptations (eye structure, forms), and the differentiation between salt-water and fresh-water species are presented as features that render the sea a provident source of food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that such precise adaptations (some fishes only in salt, others in fresh) and the variety of marine life point toward intentional provision for mankind and other creatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human engineering (e.g., Dutch dykes) highlights need for higher governance/powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The smallness of dykes compared to the sea's pressure is used as an argument that continual divine governance is necessary to preserve such lands, underscoring design and providential care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observes the Zuider-Sea, dykes AC/BD preventing overflow despite higher sea levels and ships upon it; rhetorical point that human efforts alone would be insufficient without the laws/powers God set in place.
